Gross National Product differs from Gross Domestic Product by
column2: NFIA. GNP = GDP + NFIA — the domestic-to-national adjustment of §1.1. (a) separates gross from net, which is the other axis of the grid

column1: In national accounting, the term national income refers specifically to
column2: NNP at factor cost. This is the technical definition; the loose use of "national income" for GDP is what the question is testing

column1: Net National Product is obtained from Gross National Product by deducting
column2: Depreciation — the gross-to-net adjustment. (a) would take you from GNP to GDP, sideways on the grid rather than down it

column1: If nominal GDP grows by 10% while the GDP deflator rises by 4%, real GDP grows by approximately
column2: Real growth is approximately nominal growth less the rise in the deflator: 10 − 4 = 6%. (a) adds them; (d) divides

column1: The base year of India's national accounts series has been revised to
column2: 2022-23, revised from 2011-12, with the new series drawing on ASUSE, PLFS, GST and PFMS data. §2.3 — recent enough that older material still says 2011-12

column1: Gross Value Added at basic prices, plus product taxes and less product subsidies, gives
column2: GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies. The identity in §1.2

column1: Which one of the following is not a component of the expenditure method of computing GDP?
column2: Intermediate consumption is precisely what the expenditure method excludes, to avoid double counting. The other three are all components

column1: India's official national income estimates are released by the
column2: NSO under MoSPI. The RBI publishes monetary and financial data; NITI Aayog is a think tank; the Finance Commission deals with devolution

column1: The largest contributor to India's gross value added is
column2: Services, at over half of GVA. (a) is the trap: India is agricultural in employment, not in output — §3.3

column1: The last of India's Five Year Plans was the
column2: The Twelfth, 2012–17. There has been no Thirteenth Plan; (c) exists only as a distractor

column1: The Economic Survey is prepared by the
column2: The Department of Economic Affairs under the Chief Economic Adviser, tabled the day before the Budget. (a) is the standard wrong answer, NITI Aayog being the more visible body

column1: Transfer payments such as old-age pensions are excluded from national income because
column2: No corresponding production. National income measures production; a transfer moves purchasing power without adding output. (b) is true but is not the reason

column1: According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, real GDP growth for 2025-26 was estimated in the First Advance Estimates at
column2: 7.4% in the First Advance Estimates. Note that the revised 2022-23-base series puts the year nearer 7.6%; the stem names the FAE, which is why reading which estimate is asked matters — §3.1

column1: Green GNP is a measure that adjusts conventional national income for
column2: Environmental degradation and resource depletion — the point being that output obtained by exhausting a natural asset is not equivalent to output obtained without doing so

column1: Double counting in the estimation of national income is avoided by counting
column2: Only value added at each stage. (a) and (d) are the definition of double counting; (c) explicitly includes what must be excluded

column1: Agriculture's share in India's total employment, compared with its share in gross value added, is
column2: Substantially larger — roughly 45% of employment against roughly a sixth of GVA. This is the structural anomaly of §3.3, and it is the arithmetic definition of low output per worker in agriculture

column1: The Governing Council of NITI Aayog consists of
column2: The Prime Minister, all State Chief Ministers, and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories. The Governing Council is the federal forum, which is the substantive point — NITI Aayog's design is consultative, and it does not allocate funds to States

column1: Broad money (M3) consists of M1 plus
column2: M3 = M1 + time deposits with the banking system. (a) gives M2 and (b) gives M4 — the post-office aggregates, offered together on purpose. (d) belongs to M0

column1: Narrow money (M1) is correctly described as
column2: The three components of narrow money. (b) substitutes time deposits, which would make it broad money; (d) inverts the M4 relation

column1: The Reserve Bank of India commenced operations on
column2: The Act is 1934, operations began 1 April 1935, nationalisation was 1949 — all three offered here as options for one another

column1: The Monetary Policy Committee consists of
column2: Six — three from the RBI and three external members appointed by the Central Government

column1: India's inflation-targeting framework sets the target as
column2: 4%, band of plus or minus 2 points, so a tolerance range of 2% to 6%

column1: The Cash Reserve Ratio is that proportion of a bank's net demand and time liabilities which must be
column2: A cash balance with the RBI, earning no interest. (d) is the trap: vault cash on the bank's own premises does not count towards CRR

column1: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio may be maintained in
column2: Cash, gold or approved securities, and crucially retained by the bank itself — which is the structural difference from CRR

column1: Which one of the following is a qualitative instrument of monetary policy?
column2: Margin requirements act on the terms of credit, not its volume. (a), (b) and (c) are all quantitative

column1: The floor of the Reserve Bank's liquidity adjustment facility corridor is now the
column2: The Standing Deposit Facility, which replaced the reverse repo as the floor in 2022 and is uncollateralised. (b) is the answer older material gives, which is what the question is checking

column1: The ceiling of that corridor is the
column2: The MSF, the emergency overnight window, sits at the top of the corridor. The repo rate is in the middle, not at either edge

column1: As at the August 2026 review, the policy repo rate stood at
column2: 5.25%, held unanimously at the 62nd MPC meeting of 3 to 5 August 2026, the fourth consecutive review without a change. A dated figure — re-verify

column1: Inflation brought about by a rise in the cost of inputs such as wages and oil is described as
column2: Cost-push, driven from the supply side. (a) is the demand-side counterpart, and the pair is the commonest matching item in the topic

column1: A condition in which high inflation coexists with stagnant output and high unemployment is
column2: Stagflation — the combination that ordinary demand management cannot treat, since tightening worsens the stagnation and loosening worsens the inflation

column1: The Wholesale Price Index in India is compiled and published by
column2: The Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The CPI comes from the NSO under MoSPI. (c) is the tempting answer for both, and is wrong for both

column1: The money multiplier is the ratio of
column2: M3 ÷ M0 — broad money to reserve money. It rises as the CRR falls, because banks can create more deposits per unit of reserves

column1: Fourteen major commercial banks were nationalised in India in
column2: 1969 for fourteen banks; 1980 for six more. Both years are offered, and the count is the discriminator

column1: The deposit insurance cover available per depositor per bank under the DICGC is
column2: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, raised from ₹1 lakh — so (a) is the superseded figure

column1: The priority sector lending target for domestic scheduled commercial banks is
column2: 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit. (c) 18% is the sub-target for agriculture within that 40%, which is why it is offered

column1: In order to reduce liquidity in the banking system, the Reserve Bank will
column2: Sell. Buyers pay the RBI, so money leaves the system. Selling to reduce liquidity is counter-intuitive and is the most common direction error in the topic — §2.3

column1: Statutory force was given to India's inflation-targeting framework by an amendment to
column2: The RBI Act, 1934, as amended in 2016. (a) governs banking regulation and (b) fiscal targets — plausible-sounding statutes attached to the wrong function

column1: The Annual Financial Statement is laid before Parliament under
column2: Article 112. (a) defines a Money Bill, (c) creates the Consolidated Fund and Public Account, (d) the Finance Commission — four Articles from the same chapter, offered against one another

column1: The fiscal deficit is defined as
column2: Total expenditure less total receipts EXCLUDING borrowings. (c) is the same sentence with the crucial phrase removed, and it equals zero by construction. §2.1

column1: The primary deficit is the fiscal deficit less
column2: Interest payments. The primary deficit strips out the cost of past borrowing to isolate the current year's stance

column1: The revenue deficit is the excess of
column2: Revenue expenditure over revenue receipts

column1: Which one of the following is a capital receipt of the Union Government?
column2: Recoveries of loans reduce an asset, so they are a capital receipt. (a), (c) and (d) are all revenue receipts — tax and non-tax. Apply the test: does it create a liability or reduce an asset?

column1: The Goods and Services Tax was introduced in India with effect from
column2: 1 July 2017. The 101st Amendment Act is 2016, which is why (a) and (b) are offered — the amendment year and the commencement date are different, and both get asked

column1: The GST Council is established under
column2: Article 279A. (c) Article 246A is the enabling provision giving Centre and States concurrent power to levy GST — a real and closely related Article, which makes it the best distractor

column1: Which one of the following is a direct tax?
column2: Corporation tax — its incidence cannot be shifted. The other three are indirect

column1: Following the restructuring that took effect in September 2025, GST has two principal slabs of
column2: 5% and 18%, the 12% and 28% slabs having been removed with effect from 22 September 2025 following the 56th GST Council meeting. (d) is the pre-reform pairing — §3.2

column1: Under that restructuring, a special de-merit rate applies to sin and ultra-luxury goods at
column2: 40%, the special de-merit rate for sin and ultra-luxury goods. (a) 28% is the slab it replaced for those goods

column1: With effect from 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 1961 has been replaced by
column2: The Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, the 1961 Act standing repealed subject to transitional provisions. (b) is the long-discussed Direct Taxes Code that was never enacted — a well-designed distractor

column1: The Sixteenth Finance Commission was chaired by
column2: Arvind Panagariya. (a) N K Singh chaired the Fifteenth Commission and also the FRBM review committee, which is why he is the most tempting wrong answer

column1: The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended that the States' share in the divisible pool of central taxes be fixed at
column2: 41%, unchanged from the Fifteenth Commission. (c) 42% is the Fourteenth Commission's figure — the superseded number, and the commonest error

column1: A decision of the GST Council requires the assent of
column2: Three-fourths of the weighted votes, with the Centre holding one-third and the States two-thirds — a design in which neither side can act alone

column1: A Money Bill is defined in
column2: Article 110 defines a Money Bill. (b) Article 109 lays down the procedure — the distinction between the definition and the procedure is the point of the question

column1: Expenditure from the Contingency Fund of India is incurred
column2: The President authorises it for unforeseen expenditure and Parliament regularises it afterwards. (a) reverses the sequence, which would defeat the fund's purpose

column1: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act was enacted in
column2: 2003, effective 2004. (d) 2016 is the year of inflation targeting and of the GST amendment — a plausible year attached to the wrong statute

column1: The fiscal deficit target for 2026-27 in the Union Budget was
column2: 4.3% of GDP for 2026-27 (BE), against 4.4% in 2025-26 (RE). Note (c) is the previous year's figure, so the question turns on reading which year — a dated figure, re-verify

column1: The effective revenue deficit is the revenue deficit less
column2: Grants for the creation of capital assets. The concept exists because such a grant is revenue expenditure for the Centre but finances an asset in the recipient's hands

column1: Which one of the following is constitutionally excluded from the ambit of the Goods and Services Tax?
column2: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded by the Constitution itself. Petroleum products are within GST's ambit in principle but not yet notified — a different kind of exclusion, and the reason the stem says constitutionally

column1: The Tendulkar Committee measured poverty on the basis of
column2: Monthly per capita consumption expenditure, with a mixed reference period and the inclusion of health and education spending. Tendulkar is precisely the committee that abandoned the calorie basis, so (a) describes what it moved away from

column1: Relative poverty refers to
column2: Judged against prevailing standards in the society concerned. (b) is absolute poverty — the pair is the commonest conceptual item in the topic

column1: The Human Development Index was first published in
column2: 1990, in the first Human Development Report, conceived by Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen

column1: Which one of the following does the Human Development Index not include?
column2: Unemployment is not an HDI component. The three dimensions are health, education and standard of living, and (a), (c) and (d) are the actual indicators. The HDI is deliberately austere — §3.1

column1: The Human Development Index is computed as the
column2: The geometric mean, adopted in 2010. It punishes imbalance, so very low life expectancy cannot be offset by very high income — which an arithmetic mean would permit

column1: Disguised unemployment is most characteristic of
column2: Indian agriculture, where more people are engaged than the work requires, so output would not fall if some withdrew

column1: Cyclical unemployment is caused by
column2: A downturn in aggregate demand. Cyclical unemployment disappears in recovery, which is what distinguishes it from structural

column1: The Periodic Labour Force Survey, now released monthly, is conducted by
column2: The NSO, under MoSPI. (b) the Labour Bureau conducts other labour surveys and publishes CPI-IW — a real body with a real function, attached to the wrong survey

column1: The labour force participation rate is the ratio of
column2: Labour force ÷ population. Note (d) is a meaningless ratio and (a) is the WPR — the three rates differ only in numerator and denominator, which is why they are set against one another

column1: The unemployment rate is the ratio of unemployed persons to
column2: The labour force, not the population. §2.2 — the most examined definition in the topic, and the reason the rate can fall when people stop looking for work

column1: The Physical Quality of Life Index, unlike the Human Development Index, excludes
column2: Income. The PQLI uses literacy, infant mortality and life expectancy at age one, with no income component; the HDI includes GNI per capita

column1: The Lorenz curve is used to depict
column2: The distribution of income or wealth. (a) is the Phillips curve and (d) the Laffer curve — three named curves offered together

column1: A Gini coefficient of zero indicates
column2: Perfect equality. The Gini runs from 0 (equality) to 1 (one person has everything)

column1: India's National Multidimensional Poverty Index is published by
column2: NITI Aayog publishes the National MPI; UNDP and OPHI publish the Global MPI. Both attributions get asked

column1: The three dimensions of the Multidimensional Poverty Index are
column2: Health, education and standard of living. Note that income is not a dimension — that is the entire point of a multidimensional measure, and (a) and (c) both smuggle income back in

column1: The statutory rural employment guarantee, as it stands following the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, is
column2: 125 days per rural household per financial year, under the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, in force from 1 July 2026. (c) 100 days is the superseded MGNREGA figure and is what almost all existing material still gives. Note that it remains a household entitlement and a legal guarantee, with an unemployment allowance if work is not provided within 15 days — §2.3

column1: Under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, the health cover available is
column2: ₹5 lakh per family per year. Note the unit is the family, not the individual, which is what (c) tests

column1: Replacement level fertility corresponds to a total fertility rate of about
column2: 2.1, not 2.0 — the extra tenth allows for girls who do not survive to reproductive age

column1: The first synchronous census in India was conducted in
column2: 1881, under Lord Ripon. 1872 was the first census but was non-synchronous, which is exactly what the word in the stem is testing — (a) is the answer to the question without that word

column1: The Census of India is conducted under the authority of
column2: The Census Act, 1948. Census is Entry 69 of the Union List, but the operative authority is the Act

column1: The reference date fixed for the population enumeration phase of Census 2027 for the country generally is
column2: 1 March 2027. Note that snow-bound areas have a different reference date, 1 October 2026, which is why (c) is offered — §2.3

column1: According to the Census of 2011, India's sex ratio was
column2: 943 females per 1,000 males. (a) 927 and (b) 933 are the ratios of earlier censuses, so the question is really about which census

column1: The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per
column2: Per 1,000 live births. Contrast Q7 immediately

column1: The maternal mortality ratio is expressed per
column2: Per 1,00,000 live births — a larger base than IMR because maternal deaths are far rarer. The IMR/MMR denominator pair is the commonest confusion in the topic

column1: In the theory of demographic transition, the stage in which both birth and death rates are high and population grows only slowly is
column2: The high stationary stage. Both rates high, and they offset each other. (d) also gives a stable population but with both rates low — the two stable stages, for opposite reasons

column1: The demographic dividend refers to
column2: The growth potential from a high working-age share. It is about the age structure, not the size — which is what (a) tests

column1: India's National Population Policy was adopted in
column2: 2000. (a) 1976 was the year of the coercive family planning excesses of the Emergency, a programme episode rather than a policy

column1: The economic reforms initiated in India in 1991 are commonly described as
column2: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation. (b) and (c) describe the regime the reforms dismantled

column1: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 was replaced by
column2: FEMA, 1999 — a shift from regulation to management, and from criminal prosecution to civil penalties

column1: The World Trade Organization came into existence on
column2: 1 January 1995. (a) 1948 is when GATT took effect; (c) 15 April 1994 is when the Marrakesh Agreement was signed, which is a genuinely different date from when the WTO came into being — a well-made distractor

column1: The World Trade Organization has its headquarters at
column2: Geneva. (b) Washington DC is the IMF and the World Bank, which is the standard confusion

column1: In India's balance of payments, remittances from Indians working abroad are recorded in
column2: The current account, under invisibles. Remittances are transfers, so they are neither capital account items nor net factor income from abroad — (c) is the trap for a candidate who has just read F4.1 §1.1

column1: Foreign portfolio investment differs from foreign direct investment in that it
column2: It does not confer management control, which is the definitional difference, and the reason FPI is volatile while FDI is not

column1: The Indian rupee is at present
column2: Fully convertible on the current account, not fully on the capital account. Current account convertibility dates from 1994; capital account convertibility remains partial, the Tarapore Committees' road map not having been fully implemented

column1: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were established as a result of
column2: The Bretton Woods Conference of 1944. (b) and (c) belong to the WTO — the two institutional families are set against each other here and in Q13 and Q14

column1: The dependency ratio is the ratio of
column2: The non-working-age population divided by the working-age population. It falls when the demographic dividend opens

column1: The first published description of the double-entry system is credited to
column2: Luca Pacioli, 1494, an Italian mathematician. He codified the Venetian merchants' existing practice rather than inventing it

column1: The accounting equation is
column2: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. (c) is the rearrangement done wrongly: capital is assets minus liabilities

column1: Which one of the following is a real account?
column2: Goodwill — an intangible asset, but still a real account. Real accounts are not limited to things you can touch. (a) is representative personal, (b) nominal, (d) personal

column1: Which one of the following is a nominal account?
column2: Rent Paid — an expense. Bank and Machinery are asset-type; Prepaid Insurance is representative personal

column1: Outstanding Salary Account is classified as
column2: Representative personal. The word salary pulls you to nominal, but the account stands for the employees owed. Test the party, not the title

column1: The rule for nominal accounts is
column2: Debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. (a) is the personal-account rule, (b) the real-account rule

column1: The journal is known as the
column2: Journal = book of original / prime entry

column1: The ledger is known as the
column2: Ledger = principal book, also book of final entry

column1: A contra entry is marked in the L.F. column by the letter
column2: "C", and such entries are not posted to the ledger

column1: Credit purchase of goods is recorded in the
column2: Purchases Book — but note it takes credit purchases of goods only

column1: Credit purchase of furniture by a stationery dealer is recorded in the
column2: Journal Proper. Furniture is not "goods" for a stationery dealer, so it fails the Purchases Book test even though it is a credit purchase

column1: The Sales Return Book is also called the
column2: Sales Return = Returns Inward (goods coming back in). Purchases Return = Returns Outward

column1: The three fundamental accounting assumptions are
column2: Going concern, consistency, accrual (AS-1). The items in (a) are conventions, and those in (c) are concepts — a deliberate mix

column1: A business buys machinery for cash. The effect on the accounting equation is
column2: Machinery ↑, Cash ↓. One asset becomes another; the total is unchanged. A transaction need not touch both sides of the equation

column1: If assets are ₹9,50,000 and liabilities ₹2,80,000, capital is
column2: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = 9,50,000 − 2,80,000 = ₹6,70,000. (b) adds instead of subtracting

column1: The owner withdraws ₹15,000 cash for personal use. This
column2: Drawings reduce capital but are not an expense, so profit is unaffected. This is the drawings-versus-expense distinction

column1: Under the modern classification, an increase in a liability is recorded as
column2: Liabilities increase by credit. Only assets and expenses increase by debit

column1: Which two categories of account increase by a debit?
column2: Assets and expenses — the "AE = Debit to increase" pair. Assets sit on the left of the equation, and debit is the left side

column1: A trader pays his creditor Mehta ₹80,000. The correct treatment is
column2: Debit Mehta, credit Cash. Paying a creditor settles a liability; it is not an expense. The expense arose when the goods were bought

column1: A customer deposits ₹20,000 cash into his savings account. In the bank's books
column2: In the bank's books the customer is a liability, so a deposit credits him. In the customer's own books, Bank A/c is an asset and is debited. Mirror images

column1: Cash withdrawn from the bank for the owner's personal use is
column2: Drawings. Cash withdrawn for office use is a contra entry; for personal use it is drawings. One word in the stem decides it

column1: Machinery purchased is wrongly debited to Purchases Account. This is an error of
column2: Error of principle — a capital item treated as revenue. Not commission: the giveaway is that an asset was recorded as an expense

column1: Two errors, one over-debiting an account by ₹500 and another over-crediting a different account by ₹500, constitute
column2: Compensating errors — the effects offset, so the trial balance still agrees

column1: Which one of the following will be disclosed by the trial balance?
column2: A wrong amount posted to one account only is one-sided, so debits and credits differ and the trial balance catches it. The other three are all in the "cannot catch" list

column1: Errors rectified through the Suspense Account are
column2: One-sided errors go through Suspense. Two-sided errors are corrected by a complete journal entry and never touch it

column1: Which one of the following will not be disclosed by a trial balance?
column2: A correct amount posted to a wrong account of the same class. Total debits are unchanged, so nothing unbalances. (a), (b) and (c) are all one-sided or arithmetical and therefore visible

column1: A trader buys goods on credit for ₹90,000. Which one of the following correctly describes the effect?
column2: Stock ↑ ₹90,000 (asset) and Creditors ↑ ₹90,000 (liability). No cash moved and profit is untouched — the transaction that shows profit and cash are different things

column1: The concept that treats the business as distinct from its owner is the
column2: Business entity concept. It is what makes capital a liability of the business towards the owner, and why drawings exist as a separate idea

column1: Depreciation is a direct consequence of which concept?
column2: Going concern. Because the firm will continue, the asset's cost is spread over its useful life instead of writing it down to a distress-sale value

column1: The concept that produces the accounting equation and double entry is
column2: Dual aspect — every transaction has two equal and opposite aspects, which is A = L + C and therefore double entry

column1: Under the historical cost concept, a fixed asset is recorded at
column2: The price actually paid, including costs of bringing the asset into use. (b) and (c) are the values the cost concept deliberately refuses

column1: Recording only those transactions that can be expressed in money is the
column2: Money measurement, which is why staff morale and a strong brand never appear in the accounts

column1: Valuing closing stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, illustrates
column2: Conservatism — the lower of cost and NRV never overstates the asset or the profit

column1: The convention that permits insignificant items to be ignored is
column2: Materiality. Note that it permits omission; it does not conflict with full disclosure, it defines how far disclosure must reach

column1: The Accounting Standards Board was constituted by the ICAI in
column2: 1977. Do not confuse it with 1949, the year of the Chartered Accountants Act under which ICAI itself exists

column1: Accounting Standards are prescribed by the Central Government under which section of the Companies Act, 2013?
column2: Section 133. The ASB recommends; the Central Government prescribes under s.133 in consultation with NFRA

column1: The National Financial Reporting Authority is constituted under
column2: Section 132. Sections 132 and 133 are adjacent and are a standard trap pair — 132 is the authority, 133 is the standards

column1: Capital expenditure is shown in the
column2: The Balance Sheet, as an asset. Revenue expenditure goes to the Trading or Profit and Loss account

column1: Revenue on a credit sale is recognised when
column2: When ownership passes — the realisation concept. Not on receipt of an order, and not on receipt of cash

column1: Under the accrual basis, an expense incurred but not yet paid is
column2: Recorded in the period it relates to. Ignoring it until paid is the cash basis

column1: For companies, the accrual basis of accounting is
column2: Mandatory for companies. The trap is that the cash basis sounds like a permissible simpler default

column1: The concept that makes closing stock and outstanding expenses necessary at the year end is
column2: Matching. Costs must sit in the same period as the revenues they produced, which forces every year-end adjustment

column1: The convention of consistency requires that
column2: Uniform application, with any change and its effect disclosed. (a) overstates the convention — change is allowed, concealment is not

column1: Which one of the following is a convention but not one of AS-1's fundamental assumptions?
column2: Conservatism. Consistency is both a convention and an assumption; accrual and going concern are assumptions, not conventions

column1: Under AS-1, the three fundamental accounting assumptions
column2: They are presumed followed, and disclosure is needed only when one is not. The obligation is asymmetric — silence means compliance

column1: Wages paid for the installation of a newly purchased machine are
column2: Capital. Installation wages are part of the cost of bringing the asset into use, not a running cost

column1: Carriage paid on the purchase of goods meant for resale is
column2: Revenue. Carriage on goods is consumed this period; carriage on machinery would be capital. One word decides it

column1: Repairs carried out on a second-hand machine to bring it into working condition are
column2: Capital — necessary to bring the machine into working condition. Contrast ordinary repairs to a machine already in use, which are revenue

column1: Heavy advertising expenditure to launch a new product is best treated as
column2: Deferred revenue expenditure — revenue in nature, benefit over several years, written off across them

column1: Sale proceeds of old machinery constitute
column2: A capital receipt: it reduces an asset and does not arise from normal trading

column1: Interest on a loan taken to purchase a machine, for the period before the machine is put to use, is
column2: Capitalised as part of the asset's cost, per AS 16. Interest after it is put to use is revenue

column1: Treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure will
column2: Both understated. Expenses are too high so profit is too low, and no asset was recorded so assets are too low. Both halves of the row move together

column1: In the bank's books, interest on a non-performing asset is recognised only when received. This is best described as
column2: Prudence overriding accrual. Accrual would book the earned interest; prudence refuses because collection is doubtful

column1: Under AS 15, in a defined contribution plan
column2: In a defined contribution plan the employer's obligation ends with the contribution and the employee bears investment risk. (a) and (b) describe a defined benefit plan such as gratuity

column1: The Trading Account is prepared to ascertain
column2: Gross profit. Net profit comes from the P&L; financial position from the balance sheet

column1: Which one of the following is a direct expense?
column2: Carriage inwards brings goods in, so it is a cost of making them saleable. Carriage outwards is selling and distribution

column1: Which one of the following is a fictitious asset?
column2: Preliminary expenses have no realisable value. Goodwill and patents are intangible but real; closing stock is a current asset

column1: Carriage outwards is shown in the
column2: P&L — a selling and distribution expense. Contrast carriage inwards

column1: Arranging assets and liabilities in a particular order in the balance sheet is called
column2: Marshalling. Grouping is putting similar items under one head — a different word, often the distractor

column1: Salary earned by employees but unpaid at the year end is
column2: Add to the expense (matching) and show as a current liability — you owe it. Ignoring it is the cash basis, which F6.2 §3.3 rules out for companies

column1: Insurance premium paid in advance at the year end is
column2: Deduct from the expense — it does not belong to this year — and carry it as a current asset

column1: Rent received in advance at the year end is
column2: Deduct from the income and show as a current liability: you owe the service, not the money

column1: Goods taken by the proprietor for personal use are
column2: Deduct from purchases and add to drawings. It is not a sale — no outsider bought anything — and it is not an expense of the business

column1: Every year-end adjustment has
column2: Two. Every adjustment is a journal entry, and entries have two sides. Finding only one means the adjustment is incomplete

column1: Which one of the following is not freely available for distribution as dividend?
column2: A capital reserve arises from capital profits and is not freely distributable. The other three are revenue in origin

column1: A contingent liability is
column2: Disclosed by note, not recorded. It is not yet a liability, but concealing it would mislead

column1: Provision for doubtful debts is
column2: Both effects again: debited to the P&L and deducted from debtors on the assets side

column1: Opening stock ₹40,000; purchases ₹3,00,000; purchase returns ₹10,000; wages ₹30,000; carriage inwards ₹5,000; closing stock ₹50,000; net sales ₹4,00,000. The gross profit is
column2: COGS = 40,000 + (3,00,000 − 10,000) + 30,000 + 5,000 − 50,000 = ₹3,15,000. GP = 4,00,000 − 3,15,000 = ₹85,000. Note that wages and carriage inwards are direct and belong here

column1: Net profit before charging the manager's commission is ₹4,20,000. The manager is entitled to a commission of 5% of the net profit after charging such commission. The commission is
column2: Commission after charging it: 4,20,000 × 5/105 = ₹20,000. Verify: profit after commission ₹4,00,000, and 5% of that is ₹20,000. Option (b) is 5/100, the "before" formula

column1: Sundry debtors are ₹1,00,000. Further bad debts of ₹5,000 are to be written off and a provision for doubtful debts is to be created at 5%. The provision will be
column2: Deduct the further bad debts first: 5% of (1,00,000 − 5,000) = ₹4,750. Option (a) applies the rate to the un-reduced figure — the commonest error

column1: Capital reserve is created out of
column2: Capital profits — profit on sale of a fixed asset, revaluation, profit prior to incorporation, forfeiture of shares. (c) describes reserve capital

column1: A firm's net profit is shown as ₹5,00,000. It is then found that outstanding wages of ₹30,000 had not been recorded, and that closing stock had been overvalued by ₹20,000. The corrected net profit is
column2: Both corrections reduce profit. Outstanding wages are an unrecorded expense: −30,000. Overvalued closing stock inflated gross profit, so correcting it: −20,000. 5,00,000 − 30,000 − 20,000 = ₹4,50,000

column1: Depreciation is best described as a process of
column2: Allocation. Depreciation spreads a cost already incurred over the periods benefiting from it. It does not attempt to value the asset

column1: Which one of the following is not a cause of depreciation?
column2: An increase in market value is not a cause of depreciation — and it does not remove the need to charge it, because depreciation is allocation not valuation

column1: Under the straight line method, the amount of depreciation charged each year
column2: Constant, because the rate is applied to the unchanging original cost

column1: Under the written down value method, depreciation is calculated on the
column2: The opening book value, which shrinks each year, so the charge falls

column1: The method of depreciation recognised by the Income Tax Act is the
column2: WDV is the method recognised by the Income Tax Act

column1: Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes
column2: Useful lives. Schedule XIV of the Companies Act, 1956 gave rates — the change is examinable

column1: The writing off of the cost of an intangible asset is called
column2: Amortisation for intangibles; depletion for wasting assets; depreciation for tangibles

column1: Under AS 26, goodwill is recorded in the books
column2: Only purchased goodwill. Self-generated goodwill has no reliable cost, so recording it would breach objectivity

column1: Under AS 2, inventories are valued at
column2: The lower of cost and net realisable value — conservatism in one line

column1: Which one of the following cost formulas is not permitted under AS 2?
column2: LIFO is not permitted under AS 2. FIFO, weighted average and specific identification all are

column1: Which one of the following is excluded from the cost of inventories?
column2: Selling and distribution costs. Cost covers bringing stock to its present location and condition; selling costs are incurred to move it out

column1: A machine costs ₹1,00,000, has an estimated scrap value of ₹10,000 and a useful life of 9 years. Annual depreciation under the straight line method is
column2: (1,00,000 − 10,000) ÷ 9 = ₹10,000. Option (b) divides the full cost by 9, forgetting residual value

column1: A machine costing ₹1,00,000 is depreciated at 10% on the written down value. The depreciation for the third year is
Under the written down value method, the book value of an asset
column2: Never zero, because a percentage of a positive number is always positive. It is SLM whose book value can reach zero — candidates reverse this

column1: Capital employed is ₹5,00,000, the normal rate of return is 10% and the average profit is ₹70,000. The super profit is
Super profit is ₹20,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Goodwill by the capitalisation of super profit is
column2: Capitalisation of super profit = 20,000 × 100/10 = ₹2,00,000. Option (c) applies "3 years' purchase" instead

column1: If closing stock is overvalued, the profit of the current year is
column2: Overstated. Closing stock sits on the credit of the Trading Account, so inflating it inflates gross profit

column1: In a period of rising prices, the FIFO method results in
column2: FIFO leaves the most recent and therefore highest costs in closing stock, so stock and profit are both higher

column1: A machine bought on 1 April 2021 for ₹2,00,000 is depreciated at 10% on the straight line method. It is sold on 31 March 2024 for ₹1,50,000. The result on sale is
column2: Depreciation ₹20,000 a year × 3 = ₹60,000, so WDV = ₹1,40,000. Proceeds ₹1,50,000 exceed WDV by ₹10,000 profit. Comparing proceeds with cost instead of WDV gives the ₹50,000 loss distractor

column1: Net realisable value means
column2: Estimated selling price less costs of completion and costs necessary to make the sale. NRV is neither market price (a) nor replacement cost (d)

column1: Capital employed is ₹8,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 12%. The average profit is ₹1,20,000. Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of super profit is
column2: Normal profit = 8,00,000 × 12% = ₹96,000. Super profit = 1,20,000 − 96,000 = ₹24,000. Goodwill = 24,000 × 2 = ₹48,000. Option (d) capitalises instead of multiplying by years

column1: Under Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013, the residual value of an asset is normally not to exceed
column2: 5% of original cost is the normal maximum residual value under Schedule II

column1: The ideal current ratio is generally taken as
column2: 2 : 1. Learn it paired with the quick ratio's 1 : 1, because options swap them

column1: Quick assets are current assets less
column2: Inventory and prepaid expenses. Inventory must be sold first; prepaid expenses will never become cash at all

column1: Which one of the following is a solvency ratio?
column2: Debt-equity is a long-term or solvency ratio. Current ratio is liquidity, inventory turnover is activity, gross profit is profitability

column1: The inventory turnover ratio is
column2: COGS ÷ average inventory. Option (a) drops the word average, which is the standard error

column1: The operating ratio plus the operating profit ratio equals
column2: 100. They are complements by construction, so given one you have the other

column1: Under AS 3, cash flows are classified into
column2: Operating, investing and financing. (b) names the two methods of presenting operating flows, not the classification

column1: The purchase of machinery for cash is classified as
column2: Investing — acquisition of a long-term asset

column1: For a non-financial enterprise, interest paid is classified as
column2: Financing. What you pay for capital is financing. For a bank, it would be operating

column1: For a non-financial enterprise, dividend received is classified as
column2: Investing. What you earn on investments is investing

column1: For a financial enterprise such as a bank, interest received is classified as
column2: Operating, because lending and investing are a bank's principal revenue-producing activity. This is the one place the entity's nature changes the answer

column1: Under the indirect method, depreciation is
column2: Added back, because it reduced profit without any cash leaving. Adding back is not the same as being a source of cash

column1: The issue of equity shares for cash is
column2: Financing — a change in the size of owners' capital

column1: Current assets are ₹6,00,000, including inventory ₹1,50,000 and prepaid expenses ₹50,000. Current liabilities are ₹2,00,000. The quick ratio is
column2: Quick assets = 6,00,000 − 1,50,000 − 50,000 = ₹4,00,000. Quick ratio = 4,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2 : 1. Option (d) forgets to remove prepaid expenses

column1: Net sales are ₹8,00,000 and gross profit is ₹2,00,000. The gross profit ratio is
Cost of goods sold is ₹6,00,000 and average inventory is ₹1,00,000. The inventory turnover ratio is
Capital employed is ₹10,00,000 and profit before interest and tax is ₹1,50,000. The return on capital employed is
column2: (1,50,000 ÷ 10,00,000) × 100 = 15%. Note the numerator is profit before interest and tax, matching a denominator that includes debt

column1: Which one of the following is not a limitation of ratio analysis?
column2: That is a merit — the very purpose of ratio analysis — dressed as a limitation. The other three are genuine limitations

column1: Under the Companies Act, 2013, which one of the following is not required to prepare a cash flow statement?
column2: A One Person Company is exempt, as are small companies and dormant companies

column1: A bill of exchange contains
column2: An unconditional order. A promissory note contains an unconditional undertaking — that one word generates the whole comparison table

column1: Bills of exchange in India are governed by
column2: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

column1: The number of parties to a promissory note is
column2: Two — maker and payee. A bill has three, because the order is directed at a third person

column1: Acceptance is required in the case of
column2: Only a bill of exchange. A promissory note is the maker's own promise, so there is nobody else to accept it

column1: The days of grace allowed in computing the date of maturity of a time bill are
column2: Three days, and only for time bills

column1: The maximum amount of capital a company may issue, as stated in its memorandum, is called
column2: Authorised, also called nominal or registered capital. It is the ceiling, not what has been received

column1: Under the Companies Act, 2013 the issue of shares at a discount is
column2: Prohibited and void under section 53. Option (c) echoes the repealed position under the 1956 Act

column1: A bill drawn and accepted without any trade transaction, merely to raise finance, is called
column2: An accommodation bill — no trade transaction and no consideration behind it, drawn purely to raise finance

column1: Recording the fact of the dishonour of a bill by a notary public is called
column2: Noting is the recording by a notary. Protest is the formal certificate that may follow

column1: Where a bill is paid before its due date and the holder allows a deduction, that deduction is called
column2: Rebate, allowed by the holder when the acceptor retires the bill early. Discount is what a bank deducts when the holder encashes early

column1: Interest on debentures is
column2: A charge against profit, payable regardless of profit, because debenture holders are creditors. Dividend is the appropriation

column1: That part of uncalled capital which a company resolves by special resolution to call up only in the event of winding up is called
column2: Reserve capital. Option (b) is the trap pair — capital reserve is created from capital profits

column1: Under the Companies Act, 2013 a company cannot issue
column2: Irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued under section 55. All the others may be

column1: On the reissue of forfeited shares, any balance remaining in the Forfeited Shares Account is transferred to
column2: Capital Reserve, because it is a capital profit and so cannot go to the P&L or be distributed

column1: Calls in advance received from shareholders are
column2: A liability, and expressly not available for paying dividend

column1: A bill dated 1 June 2026 is drawn for two months. Its date of maturity is
column2: 1 June + 2 months = 1 August, plus 3 days of grace = 4 August 2026. Option (b) forgets the grace days

column1: The noting charges on a dishonoured bill are ultimately borne by
column2: The drawee or acceptor, since the dishonour was his default. The drawer may pay them initially but recovers them

column1: The primary objective of an audit is
column2: To express an opinion on the true and fair view. Fraud detection is secondary — the single most reversed fact in the chapter

column1: The detection of fraud is
column2: Secondary or incidental. It follows that the auditor gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance

column1: The word "audit" is derived from a Latin word meaning
column2: Audire, to hear — accounts were once read aloud to those approving them

column1: Under the Companies Act, 2013 the auditor of a company must be
column2: A chartered accountant, or a firm where the majority of partners are so qualified — section 141

column1: The eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications of a company auditor are dealt with in
column2: Section 141. Contrast 139 appointment, 143 duties, 144 prohibited services

column1: Audit working papers are the property of
column2: The auditor's property. He may share portions at his discretion, but they are his

column1: The examination of documentary evidence in support of transactions is called
column2: Vouching examines transactions; verification examines assets and liabilities

column1: The description of an auditor as "a watchdog and not a bloodhound" comes from
column2: The Kingston Cotton Mill case. The other three are company-law cases placed there to be confused with it

column1: Standards on Auditing in India are issued by
column2: The AASB of the ICAI. Contrast accounting standards, which the ASB recommends and the Central Government prescribes under section 133

column1: Verification of an asset covers
column2: All five — existence, ownership, possession, valuation and disclosure. Valuation is part of verification, not separate from it

column1: Which one of the following is the widest in scope?
column2: Internal control is the whole system; internal check and internal audit are parts of it. Internal check is the narrowest

column1: An internal auditor is appointed by
column2: The management, which is why he is not independent of it and why his scope is set by it

column1: Internal audit is made compulsory for prescribed classes of companies by
column2: Section 138, for prescribed classes only. Section 139 is appointment of the statutory auditor

column1: Cost audit is provided for in
column2: Section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013. Section 44AB of the Income Tax Act is tax audit; section 204 is secretarial audit

column1: Examining a representative sample of transactions rather than all of them is called
column2: Test checking. Routine checking is verification of totals, postings and balances

column1: An opinion expressed where misstatements are material but not pervasive is
column2: Qualified — material but not pervasive. Pervasiveness is what escalates it

column1: An adverse opinion is expressed where misstatements are
column2: Material AND pervasive, where a misstatement is actually found

column1: A disclaimer of opinion is issued where the auditor
column2: Evidence unobtainable, with material and pervasive possible effects. Contrast the adverse opinion, where the auditor knows the statements are wrong

column1: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is dealt with in which Articles of the Constitution?
column2: Articles 148 to 151. Articles 124 to 147 concern the Supreme Court; 315 to 323 the Public Service Commissions

column1: Under section 139(2), in the case of prescribed classes of companies, an audit firm may be appointed for a maximum of
column2: Two terms of five consecutive years for a firm; an individual gets one term of five. The two limits are each other's distractors

column1: Which one of the following services may an auditor not render to the company he audits?
column2: Internal audit is prohibited by section 144, on the principle that an auditor cannot audit his own work. The other three are ordinary parts of the role

column1: A performance audit examines
column2: Economy, efficiency and effectiveness — the three Es

column1: The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General relating to the accounts of the Union are examined by
column2: The Public Accounts Committee. The Estimates Committee examines budget estimates; the COPU examines public undertakings

column1: The arithmetic mean of a set of ungrouped observations is
column2: Σx / n. Option (b) is the median, (c) the mode, (d) the range

column1: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extreme values?
column2: The arithmetic mean, because it uses every observation, so one outlier drags it. Median and mode are positional and unaffected

column1: The algebraic sum of the deviations of the observations from their arithmetic mean is
column2: Zero — Σ(x − Mean) = 0. The mean's defining property, and the reason the SD is built around it

column1: The coefficient of variation is
column2: (σ / Mean) × 100. Option (c) inverts it

column1: The empirical relationship between the three averages for a moderately skewed distribution is
column2: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean. The relationship gives the mode; solving it for the wrong quantity is the usual error

column1: In a perfectly symmetrical distribution
column2: All three coincide in a perfectly symmetrical distribution. Skewness is precisely what separates them

column1: The relationship between the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means is
column2: AM >= GM >= HM, with equality only if all observations are identical. Option (a) reverses it

column1: The mean deviation is least when measured from the
column2: The median. Contrast the sum of squared deviations, which is least from the mean — two similar results with different centres

column1: Which average can be determined graphically from an ogive?
column2: The median, from the cumulative frequency curve. The mode comes from a histogram, and the mean cannot be found graphically

column1: Which measure of dispersion is based on only two values of the series?
column2: The range uses only the two extreme values, which is both its simplicity and its weakness

column1: The standard deviation is
column2: Unaffected by origin, affected by scale. Adding a constant shifts the mean but not the scatter; multiplying scales the scatter

column1: Two series have the same mean. The series with the higher coefficient of variation is
column2: More variable and less consistent. Lower CV means greater consistency — the answer to every "which is more consistent" question

column1: The mean of 5 observations is 20. If one observation of 30 is removed, the mean of the remaining observations is
column2: Total = 5 × 20 = 100. Removing 30 leaves 70 over 4 observations = 17.5. Note the mean falls, because the removed item was above the mean

column1: One group has 20 items with a mean of 15; another has 30 items with a mean of 25. The combined mean is
column2: (20 × 15 + 30 × 25) / 50 = (300 + 750) / 50 = 21. Option (a) is the simple average of 15 and 25, which ignores the unequal group sizes — the standard trap

column1: For a moderately skewed distribution the mean is 30 and the median is 28. The mode is
Fisher's ideal index number is
column2: The geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche. It is called ideal because it satisfies both the time reversal and factor reversal tests

column1: The principle that the insured should be restored to the position occupied before the loss, and no better, is
column2: Indemnity — restoration, never betterment. Payment is the actual loss or the sum insured, whichever is lower

column1: The principle of indemnity does not apply to
column2: Life insurance, because a human life cannot be valued. It is a contract of assurance, and the same is true of personal accident cover

column1: Uberrimae fidei refers to the principle of
column2: Utmost good faith — and note the duty is mutual, not only on the insured

column1: The right of the insurer, after settling a claim, to recover from the third party responsible for the loss is called
column2: Subrogation — the insurer steps into the insured's shoes

column1: IRDAI was established under
column2: The IRDA Act, 1999. Options (a) and (b) are the two nationalisation statutes; (c) is the consolidating Act of 1938

column1: The rule that the nearest or dominant cause of a loss determines liability is
column2: Causa proxima — the proximate, not the remote, cause

column1: In life insurance, insurable interest must exist
column2: At the time of taking the policy only — you always have an interest in your own life, so nothing more is needed

column1: In marine insurance, insurable interest must exist
column2: At the time of loss, because marine cargo changes hands in transit

column1: Subrogation is a corollary of the principle of
column2: Indemnity. This is why subrogation cannot apply to life insurance — there is no measured loss to recover

column1: Under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 the scheme providing life insurance cover linked to a member's provident fund balance is
column2: EDLI, 1976. Note it is a Scheme framed under an Act — rung 3 under rung 2, in the F6.1 ladder

column1: Third-party motor insurance in India is
column2: Compulsory — third-party liability cover is mandatory under the motor vehicles law

column1: The ceiling on foreign direct investment in Indian insurance companies at present is
column2: 100%, raised from 74% by the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, effective 5 February 2026 and permitted by the automatic route. (a) 74% is the superseded figure — the ceiling set in 2021 and the one most material still gives; (c) 49% was the position before that. Note the LIC carve-out at 20% — §3

column1: The maximum assurance benefit under the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme is
column2: ₹7 lakh is the maximum assurance benefit under EDLI

column1: Under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana, the cover for accidental death or permanent total disability is
column2: ₹2 lakh for accidental death or permanent total disability; ₹1 lakh for partial disability, which is option (a) placed as the distractor

column1: Life insurance in India was nationalised by
column2: The LIC Act, 1956. The 1972 Act nationalised general insurance — sixteen years apart, and routinely swapped in options

column1: The auditor's report was candid about the lapses in record-keeping.
column2: frank. Candid means open and straightforward, even when the truth is unwelcome

column1: The officer was reticent about his reasons for reopening the inquiry.
column2: reserved. Reticent is not-forthcoming. Note it does not mean reluctant or unwilling — a common slippage

column1: The evidence produced by the inspector was cogent.
column2: convincing. Cogent argues compellingly

column1: The scheme has been defunct for several years.
column2: no longer operating. From the Latin for "having finished"

column1: She showed remarkable fortitude during the proceedings.
column2: courage in adversity. Fortitude is moral endurance, not physical strength — option (b) is the trap

column1: The employer's statements were ambiguous.
column2: open to more than one meaning. From ambi- = both (§3.1). Note it does not mean untrue

column1: The employer's conduct in concealing the records was egregious.
column2: outstandingly bad. From greg = flock (§3.2) — standing out from the herd. And the negative charge of "concealing" eliminates (a) and (c) in two seconds

column1: The witness gave a verbose account of the incident.
column2: using more words than needed. From verb = word

column1: The tribunal exonerated the employee of all charges.
column2: cleared of blame. From ex- = out of (§3.1) — out of the blame

column1: Contributions were withheld with complete impunity.
column2: freedom from punishment. Literally "without penalty"

column1: The claim was found to be spurious.
column2: false. Spurious means not genuine

column1: He gave a succinct summary of the position.
column2: brief and clear. Note the contrast with verbose in Q9 — the two are near-opposites

column1: The management was complacent about the shortfall in contributions.
column2: smugly self-satisfied. Not the same as complaisant, which means eager to please

column1: On the facts, the proposal is entirely tenable.
column2: capable of being defended. From ten = hold (§3.2) — a position that can be held. Untenable is the opposite

column1: The Commissioner refused to ______ to pressure from the employer.
column2: accede = to yield or agree. Exceed is to go beyond — the confusable pair from §4

column1: His remarks were ______ to the issue and helped settle it.
column2: germane = relevant. Note the continuation signal "and helped settle it", which requires a positive, relevant word — so extraneous and redundant are ruled out by §2.2

column1: The vehicle remained ______ at the crossing for several minutes.
column2: stationary = not moving. Station-e-ry with an e is for envelopes

column1: The auditor's role is to ______ the accounts, not to prepare them.
column2: scrutinise. Proscribe forbids, prescribe recommends — neither is what an auditor does. This is F6.7's point that audit examines rather than prepares

column1: The employer attempted to ______ the statute by reclassifying wages as allowances.
column2: circumvent = to get around. From circum- = around (§3.1). Note the negative charge of the sentence

column1: It is a matter of ______, not of money.
column2: principle = a rule or belief, and the slot after "a matter of" needs a noun (§2.4). The rule ends in -le

column1: The two sets of accounts were ______ to identify the discrepancy.
column2: reconciled — brought into agreement. Rescinded means cancelled

column1: The order of the lower authority was ______ by the appellate authority.
column2: rescinded = cancelled. Ratified is the opposite — approved; remanded means sent back

column1: A decision is ______; it is expected to be announced today.
column2: imminent = about to happen. Eminent is distinguished; immanent means inherent

column1: The report was strongly ______ of the department's handling of the case.
column2: censorious = severely critical. The signal word "strongly" plus the negative framing rules out laudatory and neutral

column1: Notwithstanding the employer's ______ protestations of compliance, the inspection revealed systematic under-reporting.
column2: vehement. "Notwithstanding" signals contrast (§2.2): the protestations must have been forceful for the contrast with the finding to bite. Vehement protestations is also the natural collocation (§2.5)

column1: The scheme, though well intentioned, proved to be a damp squib. The idiom means
column2: a disappointing anticlimax — something that fails to go off, like a firework that has got wet

column1: The determination was made ex parte, which means
column2: in the absence of one of the parties — and, as §6 notes, an ex parte Section 7A order is exactly this

column1: The employer's explanation strained credulity, meaning that it was
column2: difficult to believe. From cred = believe (§3.2)

column1: Far from being ______, the penalty was widely regarded as lenient.
column2: draconian. "Far from" signals contrast, and the other half says lenient — so the blank must be its opposite. The sentence supplies the answer without any vocabulary at all (§2.2)

column1: The two provisions are not in conflict with each other; they are ______.
column2: complementary — completing each other. Note the spelling: complementary completes, complimentary praises

column1: To describe something as a moot point is to say that it is
column2: open to debate. The commonest error is to read moot as "settled" or "irrelevant"

column1: P. This makes them unsuitable for use in hard water. Q. Soaps are the sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids. R. Detergents were developed to overcome this limitation. S. They form an insoluble scum with calcium and magnesium ions.
column2: Q S P R. Q names soaps; S's "They" refers to them; P's "This" refers to the scum in S; R's "this limitation" refers to P. A chain of three back-references, each fixing one position

column1: P. Momentum, however, is conserved in every collision. Q. Collisions are classified as elastic or inelastic. R. In an inelastic collision kinetic energy is not conserved. S. In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
column2: Q S R P. Q announces the two categories; S and R take them in the order named; P's "however" contradicts R. "However" almost never opens

column1: P. A provision is therefore created even when the year results in a loss. Q. A provision is a charge against profit. R. A reserve, by contrast, is an appropriation of profit. S. It can be created only if there is a profit.
column2: Q P R S. Q states the charge; P's "therefore" follows from it; R's "by contrast" introduces the reserve; S's "It" refers to the reserve, so S must follow R

column1: P. Each of these is exactly three binary digits. Q. The octal system uses the digits 0 to 7. R. Conversion between binary and octal therefore requires no arithmetic. S. Grouping the bits in threes from the right is sufficient.
column2: Q P R S. Q names the digits; P's "Each of these" refers to them; R's "therefore" draws the conclusion; S explains how

column1: P. He must issue notice, hear the employer and pass a reasoned order. Q. An Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner conducts inquiries under Section 7A. R. That function is therefore described as quasi-judicial. S. The order so passed is appealable.
column2: Q P S R. Q introduces the officer; P describes what he must do; S adds that the order is appealable; R's "That function is therefore" concludes from all of it

column1: P. The trial balance will nevertheless agree. Q. An error of principle arises when a capital item is treated as revenue. R. Both the profit and the assets are understated. S. The entry is balanced, though wrongly classified.
column2: Q R S P. Q defines the error; R gives the effect; S explains why the entry balances; P's "nevertheless" states the consequence for the trial balance, which only makes sense after S

column1: P. This band deliberately straddles neutral. Q. Industrial effluent discharged into inland surface water must fall within a permissible pH range. R. Requiring exact neutrality would be unattainable in practice. S. That range is about 5.5 to 9.0.
column2: Q S P R. Q introduces the range; S's "That range" is a mandatory pair with Q; P's "This band" refers to S; R explains why the band is wide

column1: P. Each node must be connected to every other node. Q. A mesh topology is the most reliable of the network topologies. R. The number of links required is therefore n(n − 1)/2. S. Every link would otherwise be counted twice, once from each end.
column2: Q P R S. Q introduces mesh; P states the requirement; R's "therefore" gives the formula; S's "otherwise" explains the division by two, which only makes sense once the formula is on the table

column1: P. Detergents, by contrast, are less readily biodegradable. Q. Their branched chains resist breakdown and cause foaming in rivers. R. Soaps are biodegradable. S. Environmental regulation therefore followed the technology rather than preceding it.
column2: R P Q S. R opens — the only sentence with no back-reference. P's "by contrast" must follow R; Q's "Their" refers to the detergents in P; S's "therefore" concludes

column1: P. It must respond within a strict and guaranteed deadline. Q. A real-time operating system is not defined by being fast. R. Predictability, rather than average speed, is the requirement. S. Air traffic control is a typical application.
column2: Q P R S. Q makes the negative claim; P states what the definition actually is; R restates it as a contrast; S illustrates. General before specific puts the example last

column1: Which sentence should come first?
column2: Q. P begins "This is why", R says "in it", S says "The first stage" — all three depend on something earlier. Only Q stands alone

column1: Which sentence should come last?
column2: P. "This is why" summarises the consequence of everything preceding, and no sentence in the set follows from P. The full order is Q S R P

column1: P. Only about a tenth of it passes to the next trophic level. Q. Energy enters an ecosystem through the producers. R. Food chains are consequently short. S. The remainder is lost as heat and in metabolism.
column2: Q P S R. Q introduces the energy; P's "it" refers to that energy; S accounts for "the remainder", which only exists once P has named a tenth; R's "consequently" concludes

column1: The passage is mainly concerned with
column2: Claim plus qualification, which §3.4 says is nearly always the shape of the right option. (a) and (d) are contradicted — the author never ranks the two models, and says popular discussion blurs the distinction. (b) is the recommendation the passage explicitly rejects in its last clause

column1: According to the passage, social assistance is financed from
column2: Explicit: "financed from general revenues". (b) is the definition of social insurance, offered as Pattern 4 — the passage's own words attached to the wrong category

column1: It follows from the passage that an amendment raising the wage ceiling would
column2: The last sentence says extending coverage needs redefinition or a shift of model, "and not merely an amendment raising the wage ceiling", and the reason is given: the unorganised worker lacks a contributing employer. (a) reverses the passage. (b) and (c) add facts the passage does not supply

column1: The word blurred as used in the passage means
column2: Vocabulary in context. Blurred here describes a distinction not clearly drawn; (a) imputes deliberate concealment, which the sentence does not — the author blames imprecision, not bad faith. §3.3's rule: the sentence decides

column1: The author's purpose is best described as
column2: The structure is a correction ("often blurred") followed by a consequence ("This has a consequence that critics frequently overlook"). (b) overstates — the author defends the Act's logic. (d) is the option the last sentence forecloses

column1: According to the passage, the auditor's report is
column2: Explicit: "The outcome is an opinion, not a certificate." (a) and (c) are the two guarantees the passage denies; (d) reverses the independence point in the first paragraph

column1: The passage implies that an audit which failed to detect a well-concealed fraud
column2: The passage states it almost in terms: failure to uncover a concealed fraud "does not by itself establish that the audit was inadequate", because adequacy depends on what was done. (a) is the reversal; (b) and (c) are Pattern 3, outside the passage entirely

column1: The word persuasive as used in the passage means
column2: The word is defined by its own contrast in the sentence — "persuasive rather than conclusive". This is the clearest possible case of §3.3: the adjacent word settles it

column1: Which one of the following is not stated or implied in the passage?
column2: The "not" question. The passage says the opposite: "the auditor neither prepares the accounts nor manages the enterprise." (b), (c) and (d) are each stated. Note that reading only the first four words of the stem loses this mark — Blueprint §8's habit

column1: The author's principal purpose in the passage is to
column2: The second paragraph opens by announcing exactly this: "The reason for this modest phrasing is evidential rather than diplomatic." (a) inverts the author's sympathy; (b) is too narrow, procedures being mentioned only as evidence; (c) is contradicted

column1: According to the passage, the surface pH of the ocean has fallen
column2: Explicit. (c) is Pattern 4 — thirty per cent belongs to hydrogen ion concentration, not to pH, and the two are related logarithmically. (b) and (d) contradict "Seawater at pH 8.1 is alkaline"

column1: On the passage's own account, the term ocean acidification is imprecise because
column2: The passage's own reason: the water is alkaline and is not projected to become acidic. (b) is a true statement from the passage, but it is the reason the change is significant, not the reason the name is imprecise — Pattern 6, the right answer to a different question

column1: The word sink, if used in this passage to describe the ocean, would most nearly mean
column2: Vocabulary in context, tested on a word the passage does not use, which forces you to reason from the described function: the ocean takes up and retains carbon dioxide. (a) is wrong because the carbon is not destroyed; the passage traces exactly what becomes of it

column1: It can be inferred from the passage that the author regards the objection that the ocean is not becoming an acid as
column2: The last sentence: those who minimise the problem "point out, correctly, that the ocean is not becoming an acid, and treat the correction as though it disposed of the argument." Correct, but not an answer. (a) and (b) both call it mistaken; the author expressly concedes it is right. (c) is what the author is arguing against

column1: The author's tone in the passage is best described as
column2: The passage explains, distinguishes and qualifies; it never raises its voice. §3.5's rule that the milder tone option wins in this register. (a) is the tempting overreach, given the final sentence's evident impatience

column1: The passage is mainly about
column2: Claim plus response, covering both paragraphs. (d) is Pattern 1's cousin, too narrow — the contribution rate is one detail. (a) is the question the last sentence explicitly sets aside. (b) is never discussed

column1: According to the passage, the aggregator's contribution is fixed as
column2: Explicit, and the detail matters: a percentage of turnover, capped by reference to what is paid to workers. (a) reverses who pays; (c) and (d) are plausible mechanisms the passage does not mention — Pattern 3

column1: The passage implies that the central difficulty the platform economy creates for social insurance is that
column2: The first paragraph's whole point: the person works, often for a single controlling entity, but the obligation "has no natural place to attach." (b), (c) and (d) may be true in the world and are the trap of §4.3 — none is in the passage

column1: The word attenuated as used in the passage means
column2: Attenuated means thinned or weakened. The passage confirms the sense by contrast: the relationship is attenuated, so the Code responds "not by asserting that platform workers are employees" — weakened, not abolished, which is why (a) fails

column1: The last sentence of the passage suggests that the author regards the Code's approach as
column2: "Whether that yields adequate benefits is a separate question from whether it yields any, and it is the second question the Code was drafted to answer." That is a defence of the Code's modest ambition, so (a) overstates and (b) and (d) misread the author's sympathy

column1: The list of members whose contributions are in arrears **
column2: has been placed. The subject is the list, not members — §2.1 rule 1. The intervening phrase is there precisely so that a plural noun sits next to the verb

column1: Each of the three schemes have **
column2: has been framed. Each of is singular — rule 4 — whatever follows it

column1: The number of establishments **
column2: has risen. The number of is singular; a number of would be plural — rule 6. One article decides the verb

column1: Hardly had the inspection begun than **
column2: Hardly had the inspection begun when. Hardly and scarcely pair with when; only no sooner takes than (§3.1). Compare Q26

column1: The auditor stated that **
column2: he would submit. A past reporting verb (stated) pulls the reported verb back — §3.2's second point. The report is not a universal truth, so the exception does not apply

column1: The Commissioner directed **
column2: to return the registers. Return back is a redundancy (§6.3) — return already contains back

column1: The two provisions differ ______ each other in one respect only.
column2: differ from. Things differ from each other; you differ with a person, on a point — §4.1

column1: The inquiry into the default was entrusted ______ an Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner.
column2: entrusted with. A person is entrusted with a task; a task is entrusted to a person. Here the officer is entrusted, so with. This pair is worth memorising in both directions

column1: The gravity of the offence consists ______ the deliberate withholding of contributions already deducted.
column2: consists in. Consist in = has its essence in; consist of = is made up of. The gravity of an offence is its essence, not its parts

column1: A member who has contributed for the required period is entitled ______ the pension as a matter of right.
column2: entitled to. One of the fixed to list in §4.2, alongside superior, inferior, senior, preferable, averse

column1: The inspector insisted ______ examining the original wage registers.
column2: insisted on. Insist takes on; insist to and insist about do not exist

column1: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
column2: The police have. Police is a singular-looking plural, with people, cattle, gentry, clergy, vermin, poultry — rule 10. All three wrong options use a singular verb

column1: Which one of the following sentences is correct?
column2: senior to. Superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, preferable take to, never than — §6.2. (c) adds a second error: senior is already comparative, so more senior is a double comparative

column1: He is one of the few officers who ______ willing to record a dissent.
column2: who are. The relative clause describes the few officers, not one — rule 11. This is the agreement rule that sounds wrong to nearly everyone and is therefore examined

column1: There were ______ defaults this year than last, and consequently ______ money had to be recovered by coercive process.
column2: fewer defaults, less money. Fewer counts, less measures — §6.2. Defaults can be counted; money as an amount cannot

column1: If A's salary is 25% more than B's, then B's salary is less than A's by
column2: A = 1.25B, so the difference is 0.25B on a base of A, not B: 0.25/1.25 = 20%. §1.3 result 1. Option (a) is the answer to a question about the other direction

column1: An increase of 16⅔% is the same as multiplying by
column2: 16⅔% = 1/6, so an increase multiplies by 1 + 1/6 = 7/6. This is the fraction habit that pays throughout the chapter

column1: ₹6,300 is divided among three persons in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. The largest share is
column2: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts; one part = 6,300/9 = 700; largest = 4 × 700 = ₹2,800. Note (b) is 3 parts and (a) is 2 — the wrong-share trap

column1: The average weight of 8 men is 62 kg. One man weighing 55 kg is replaced by another and the average becomes 63 kg. The weight of the new man is
column2: The average rose 1 kg over 8 men, so the total rose 8 kg: 55 + 8 = 63 kg. §3.2's rule in one line, and the 2023 "mean of weights" shape

column1: The ages of A and B are in the ratio 4 : 3 and their sum is 42 years. A's age is
column2: 4 + 3 = 7 parts for 42 years, so one part = 6 and A = 4 × 6 = 24. (a) is B's age — always check whose was asked

column1: 40 litres of a mixture contain milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. The quantity of water is
column2: Water is 1 part of 4: 40 × 1/4 = 10 litres. (d) is 3/4, the milk

column1: A can do a piece of work in 12 days and B in 18 days. Working together they will finish it in
column2: LCM 36 units; A does 3 a day, B 2, together 5. 36/5 = 7.2 days. Adding the days to get 30, or averaging them to 15, are the two standard errors — (d) is the average

column1: A sum is first reduced by 20% and then increased by 20%. The net change is
column2: 0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96, a 4% decrease. §1.3 result 2: down-then-up by the same percentage is always a loss of x²/100, here 400/100. (a) is the intuitive wrong answer

column1: If a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5, then a : c is
column2: Make b common: a : b = 8 : 12 and b : c = 12 : 15, so a : b : c = 8 : 12 : 15 and a : c = 8 : 15

column1: The average of 11 results is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and of the last six is 52. The sixth result is
column2: 6 × 49 + 6 × 52 = 606, against a whole of 11 × 50 = 550. The sixth result is counted twice, so it is 606 − 550 = 56. §3.3's overlap trick

column1: A father is three times as old as his son. After 12 years he will be twice as old as his son. The son's present age is
column2: 3s + 12 = 2(s + 12) gives s = 12. Check: 36 and 12 become 48 and 24, which is 2 : 1

column1: An employee's share of contribution is 12% of basic wages of ₹18,000. The amount deducted is
Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% are equivalent to a single discount of
column2: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so a single discount of 28%. (b) is the sum of the two discounts, which is always wrong because the second discount applies to a reduced price

column1: In what ratio must milk costing ₹40 a litre be mixed with water, which costs nothing, so that the mixture costs ₹32 a litre?
column2: Alligation on price: (32 − 0) : (40 − 32) = 32 : 8 = 4 : 1. Sense check: the mixture costs 4/5 of the milk price, so it must be 4/5 milk

column1: A and B together can complete a work in 8 days, and A alone can complete it in 12 days. B alone will take
